rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window, retain weakly retained compounds, and identify critical unresolved pairs. A midrange temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to test whether the critical pair at 4.88–4.95 min responds to a shallower slope. The other pairs have resolution to spare, so this comparison will guide slope optimization versus temperature tuning.

Shift the starting organic fraction upward while keeping the slope close to the fully resolving second run. This should bring the last peak below 10 minutes while largely preserving the critical pair’s resolution.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to lift the critical pair above R = 1.5, while raising the starting organic fraction to keep the last peak below 10 minutes. The early pairs have ample resolution to accommodate some compression.

Keep the starting composition fixed and lower the endpoint to make the gradient shallower without another starting-composition selectivity shift. This should improve the critical pair’s resolution while using the remaining 0.92-minute margin below the time penalty threshold.
The maximum CRF is already achieved; test a 5 °C temperature increase to seek a shorter fully resolved run. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates temperature’s effect on the critical pair.

Test whether a larger temperature increase carries the critical pair through its selectivity crossover and restores separation while shortening retention. Injection 5 remains the maximum-score fallback; inspect all pairs for new overlaps after reordering.

At 60 °C the former critical region is resolved, but a different pair nearly co-elutes. Test 55 °C to seek a selectivity window where both regions are resolved while retaining a shorter run than injection 5.

Slightly flatten the gradient at 55 °C to try to raise the new critical pair from R = 1.41 above 1.5. Check that the pair currently at R = 1.74 remains resolved; the last peak has ample margin below 10 minutes.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving injection 9’s slope to seek a shorter maximum-score method. Monitor both close middle pairs and the early peaks, since the higher starting organic fraction can change selectivity and compress early separation.

Lower the starting organic fraction to improve early retention and potentially recover separation of the new critical pair. Combine this with a steeper gradient to seek a shorter fully resolved run than injection 9.

Increase the endpoint by one grid step to shorten the fully resolved 8-minute elution window. This modest steepening tests whether both close middle pairs remain above R = 1.5 while preserving the maximum CRF.

Lowering the starting organic fraction may recover the critical pair’s selectivity, while increasing the endpoint offsets the added retention. Test whether this shifted, steeper gradient preserves full resolution with a last peak earlier than injection 11’s 8.00 minutes.

Test a shorter gradient against injection 13 to establish the speed limit at this temperature and starting composition. The maximum CRF is already secured; this run checks whether further time savings are possible without sacrificing either close middle pair.

Explore a substantially steeper gradient at 60 °C to test whether the troublesome middle pair separates on the opposite side of its selectivity crossover. This targets a faster fully resolved method while retaining the established maximum-score methods as fallbacks.

Shorten only the gradient to test whether further steepening separates the remaining critical pair on this high-temperature branch. Monitor its neighboring pair, currently at R = 1.62, for a competing loss of resolution.

Explore the untested low-temperature selectivity regime rather than further compressing the competing pairs at 60 °C. A broad, moderately steep gradient should limit retention while testing whether reordered middle peaks permit another fully resolved method.

Test an intermediate low-temperature regime with a faster gradient to seek favorable selectivity between the crowded 25 °C pattern and the successful 40 °C regime. This explores another route to a shorter fully resolved run while the maximum-score methods remain available.

Trim injection 13’s unused high-organic tail while preserving its starting composition and gradient slope exactly. The last peak’s estimated elution composition is about 0.57, so all peaks should remain within the gradient and retain the maximum CRF.

Seek a larger resolution margin at the maximum CRF by slightly flattening injection 9’s gradient. Its two closest pairs responded favorably or changed little with the previous slope reduction, and the last peak should remain below 10 minutes.

Use a slope between injections 11 and 12 to target full resolution with a shorter elution time than injection 11. The estimated last-peak elution composition is below 0.60, so the trimmed endpoint should comfortably retain all peaks within the gradient.

Test a slightly shallower gradient than injection 11 to seek more separation margin while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes. This should improve the slope-sensitive pair, but the other close pair must be checked because its resolution decreases slightly as the gradient flattens.

Choose a slope between injections 9 and 20 to balance their two closest pairs, targeting a minimum resolution near 1.7 while retaining CRF 1.000. The trimmed endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition.

Use a slope between injections 20 and 23 to balance the two limiting pairs near R = 1.7. This targets additional resolution margin while keeping the predicted last peak below 10 minutes and preserving the maximum CRF.

Trim the unused high-organic tail of injection 24 with a nearly identical slope, targeting balanced critical-pair resolutions near 1.7 and a last peak around 9.3 minutes. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition, so this shorter programmed gradient should preserve CRF 1.000.
